design_detail: Reply letter (PNAS 110(11):E980–E982, online 4 March 2013) by four authors of Meier et al. (2012), answering Rogeberg (2013) and a letter by Daly (2013, PNAS E979, not read). It reports new analyses of the Dunedin birth cohort: family SES (three classes by the breadwinner's occupation, illustrated by example occupations; the measure and the age at which it was assessed are not stated) as a predictor of adolescent-onset cannabis dependence and of IQ change; the 2012 linear-trend model of full-scale IQ change on waves of cannabis dependence with SES or childhood self-control added; and the same model restricted to the 553 members from middle-class families. Filed as prospective-cohort, the design of the data reanalysed, because its results are new individual-level analyses of that cohort; its argumentative passages are cited as the authors' position.
can_establish: Whether, in the Dunedin cohort, family SES as classified here and childhood self-control predicted adolescent-onset cannabis dependence or IQ change, and whether adding either to the 2012 model, or restricting it to middle-class families, changed the association between persistent cannabis dependence and IQ decline.
cannot_establish: That no confounding explains the association, because SES and self-control are each added alone to the sex-only model, never together or with the other-substance covariates of the 2012 multivariable model, and family, genetic and childhood behavioural factors beyond these two are not examined; nor does it report the pre-exposure IQ trajectory test that Rogeberg proposed.

sample.recruitment: Dunedin birth cohort (card sc_meier_2012): consecutive births in Dunedin, New Zealand, 1972–1973; the analyses use the 874 members of the 2012 analysis (Fig. 2 key).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As in Meier et al. (2012). The middle-class restriction excludes families whose breadwinner had a low-skill occupation (foodpacker is the example given) or a professional one (dentist); middle class is illustrated by building inspector and aircraft mechanic (3rd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not reported in the letter; no table by SES class or by exposure group.
sample.attrition: Not reported in the letter; the analyses inherit the 2012 sample.
sample.selection_effects: As in the original cohort. The middle-class restriction keeps 553 of 874 (63%, editors' arithmetic) and leaves 8 to 32 people per cell in the age-of-onset comparison (Fig. 3B); 553 and the cell sizes are figure values read by the first reader only.

exposure.measurement: As in Meier et al. (2012): waves of DSM cannabis dependence between 18 and 38 (five-level exposure), and adolescent-onset dependence (dependence before 18).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As in Meier et al. (2012); not restated in the letter.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed in the new analyses: the SES- and self-control-adjusted models are compared with the sex-only model (β = −0.152, t = −4.45), not with the 2012 multivariable model that also adjusted for other dependence, recent use and schizophrenia (t = −2.20).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: As in Meier et al. (2012); not addressed.

comparison.controls: Cohort members who never used cannabis, in the full cohort or within the middle-class subsample (Fig. 2).
comparison.matching: None; SES or self-control is added as a covariate, or SES is held roughly constant by restriction to middle-class families.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family SES and childhood self-control, both measured before cannabis use, are now examined. Still not examined: family psychiatric history, genetic liability, parenting, childhood conduct or attention problems, and peers.

outcomes.instruments: Full-scale IQ change from childhood (ages 7–13) to 38, as in 2012; for the SES trajectories, mean full-scale IQ at 7, 9, 11, 13 and 38 by SES class (Fig. 1); adolescent-onset dependence as the outcome of SES in one test.
outcomes.operationalization: Confounding is judged by (a) whether SES predicts adolescent-onset dependence, (b) whether SES or self-control correlates with IQ change, and (c) whether the trend coefficient changes when SES or self-control is added or when the sample is restricted to middle-class families.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; a handful of tests on two outcomes (full-scale IQ change and adolescent-onset dependence).

analysis.effect_sizes: SES and adolescent-onset dependence: χ2 = 1.15, P = 0.56 (df not given; with three SES classes df = 2 reproduces P = 0.56, editors' check); 23% of the adolescents who used cannabis came from low-SES families (denominator and cohort share of low SES not given). SES and IQ change from adolescence to adulthood: r = −0.006, P = 0.86. Trend coefficient of IQ change on waves of dependence: β = −0.152 (t = −4.45, P < 0.0001) with sex only; β = −0.158 (t = −4.58, P < 0.0001) with SES added; β = −0.155 (t = −3.61, P = 0.0003) among the 553 from middle-class families (553 read from Fig. 2 by the first reader only). Childhood self-control and IQ decline: r = −0.034, P = 0.31; trend with self-control added β = −0.151 (t = −4.38, printed P = 0.0001). β is not defined (standardized or not) and no confidence intervals are given. Read approximately from the rendered Fig. 2: 3 or more waves of dependence about −0.38 SD in the full cohort and about −0.37 SD in the middle-class subsample; never used about +0.05 and +0.07.
analysis.covariates: Sex, as in 2012, plus SES or plus childhood self-control, one at a time.
analysis.selective_reporting: The tests were chosen to answer the two critiques. Not shown: the SES distribution of the cohort and of each exposure group, a model with SES, self-control and the other-substance covariates together, any test of the adolescent-onset contrast within the middle-class subsample (Fig. 3B shows bars only), and the data behind the statement that tests more susceptible to SES did not show more decline (3rd paragraph).
analysis.power: Not addressed; the middle-class age-of-onset cells hold 8 to 32 people (Fig. 3B, first reader's reading).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the Dunedin data, family SES class did not significantly predict adolescent-onset dependence and was unrelated to IQ change from adolescence to 38; adding SES or childhood self-control to the sex-adjusted model, or restricting to middle-class families, left the trend coefficient essentially unchanged (−0.152 against −0.158, −0.155 and −0.151).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title announces "No evidence that socioeconomic status or personality differences confound" the association, and the text says the data exclude SES as the explanation and that the tests exclude initial differences in conscientiousness. Gaps: (1) these are tests of two specific measures, each added alone to a sex-only model; they exclude these measures as explanations, not confounding in general; (2) the SES measure is three occupational classes, neither defined nor dated in the letter, and the 23% figure has no base rate; (3) the letter describes the within-individual change design as controlling for any and all childhood influences (5th paragraph), which holds for stable differences only, the point at issue in Rogeberg's critique; (4) the statement that SES-sensitive tests did not decline more is made without data; (5) personality is represented by childhood self-control, which the letter calls a precursor of conscientiousness. Against this, the tests are direct, use measures taken before cannabis use, and the letter acknowledges that observational studies cannot prove causation.

timeline.event: Meier et al. (Dunedin), the study defended (card sc_meier_2012).
Rogeberg (PNAS 110:4251–4254): simulation of SES confounding, answered here (card sc_rogeberg_2013).

Daly, letter proposing that conscientiousness may explain the association (PNAS 110:E979; not read). This reply says Daly's own test in the National Child Development Study did not confirm the idea and that its personality measure was taken at 50, after cannabis use (4th paragraph).
A rejoinder titled Reply to Moffitt et al.: Causal inference from observational data remains difficult (PNAS 110:E983), linked from this letter's page; not read.

Jackson et al., two US twin cohorts: adjustment for a composite SES measure did not attenuate the cannabis–vocabulary association, consistent with this reply on SES, but twins who used did not differ significantly from co-twins who did not, which the authors read as familial confounding other than SES (card sc_jackson_2016). Jackson et al. cite Rogeberg (2013) but not this reply.

Meier et al. (Addiction), a longitudinal co-twin control study of adolescent cannabis use and neuropsychological decline, in the project's Tier A list and carded in this round by another reader; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: On its narrow question the reply is direct and largely convincing: in Dunedin, family SES as classified did not predict adolescent-onset dependence or IQ change, and adding it or restricting to middle-class families left the association unchanged; Jackson et al. (2016) likewise found no attenuation by SES in two US cohorts. It does not settle the wider question of confounding: no joint model is reported, the pre-exposure trajectory test Rogeberg proposed is not reported, and within-family comparisons in other cohorts (Jackson et al., 2016; later co-twin studies in the project's lists, not read here) point to family factors beyond SES.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the letter; the funders of the 2012 study are on card sc_meier_2012.
funding.declared_conflicts: "The authors declare no conflict of interest." (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors are authors of the study under criticism (M.H.M. first author; T.E.M. senior author), at Duke University, the Institute of Psychiatry at King's College London and the Dunedin unit of the University of Otago; all four designed, performed and analysed the new analyses and wrote the letter (author contributions). The letter defends the authors' own study, a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: One model of the Dunedin data adjusting jointly for family SES, childhood self-control, conduct problems, family psychiatric history and other substance dependence, reported with coefficients and intervals; the pre-exposure IQ trajectory test Rogeberg proposed (IQ from 7 to 13 by later exposure group); and within-family comparisons (twins or siblings discordant for persistent adolescent-onset dependence) followed into midlife.

domains.note: Adds family SES (three occupational classes) and childhood self-control, each alone, to a sex-only model; no joint model, and the other-substance covariates of the 2012 multivariable model are not carried over; genetic and family liability and childhood conduct problems remain uncontrolled. For the narrower question whether SES as classified explains the association, the tests are direct and at lower risk.
As in 2012: prospective structured diagnoses, self-reported and unverified.
Population birth cohort; the middle-class restriction is a deliberate analytic choice.
As in 2012 (874 of about 964 members assessed at 38); the numbers in each SES class and in the χ2 and correlation analyses are not given.
As in 2012: different Wechsler versions in childhood and at 38; testers' blinding not reported. The SES measure is not defined in the letter.
Analyses chosen to rebut two critiques; base rates, the joint model and the data behind the SES-sensitive-test statement are not shown; β is undefined and no intervals are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain. The reply addresses the two named confounders directly with measures taken before cannabis use, and on that narrow question it is informative: the coefficient barely moves. But each confounder is added alone, and other plausible confounders are not addressed, so the result does not lower the risk of confounding for the causal question as a whole. Citable for the SES and self-control tests and their coefficients, the middle-class restriction (n=553) and the SES trajectories in Fig. 1; not for the claim that confounding has been excluded in general.

key_findings.finding: Low family SES did not significantly predict adolescent-onset cannabis dependence (χ2 = 1.15, P = 0.56); 23% of the adolescents who used cannabis came from low-SES families, defined by the breadwinner's low-skill occupation (foodpacker is the example).
key_findings.note: Neither the share of low-SES families in the cohort nor the number of adolescents who used cannabis is given, so whether 23% is an over- or under-representation cannot be judged; the χ2 concerns adolescent-onset dependence, the 23% any adolescent cannabis use. The test is not significant in a small group (the 2012 paper's Fig. 2 shows 52 people with dependence before 18: 17 + 12 + 23, editors' sum), so it shows no significant association, not the absence of one.

key_findings.finding: IQ of children from low-SES families did not change from the beginning of schooling to adolescence or from adolescence to adulthood, and low SES was unrelated to adolescent-to-adult IQ decline (r = −0.006, P = 0.86). In Fig. 1, mean IQ by SES class at ages 7, 9, 11, 13 and 38 runs roughly flat: about 94 to 92 (low), 101 to 100 (middle) and 110 to 110 (high).
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 values read approximately from the rendered figure by the first reader only; the second reader and the adjudicator could not view the image (deferred: figure image not viewable). The first reader saw no group sizes or error bars. The series starts at age 7, so it cannot show change from before school entry.

key_findings.finding: Trend of full-scale IQ change on waves of cannabis dependence: β = −0.152 (t = −4.45, P < 0.0001) for the 2012 model, whose paper printed only the t; with SES added β = −0.158 (t = −4.58, P < 0.0001).
key_findings.note: β is not defined as standardized or unstandardized; the comparison model is the sex-only model, not the 2012 multivariable model (t = −2.20).

key_findings.finding: Restricted to the 553 members from middle-class families (excluding low-SES and high-SES families), the trend was β = −0.155 (t = −3.61, P = 0.0003), and the group means followed the full-cohort pattern (3 or more waves of dependence about −0.37 SD against about −0.38 in the full cohort of 874).
key_findings.note: The text confirms the restriction to middle-class families (low- and high-SES families left out) and β = −0.155, t = −3.61, P = 0.0003. The n of 553 and the bar values are printed only in Fig. 2 and were read by the first reader only; the second reader and the adjudicator could not view the image (deferred: figure image not viewable). A back-calculation from β and t (second reader) makes an n near 550 plausible. Group sizes within the middle-class subsample are not shown.

key_findings.finding: Fig. 3B restricts the age-of-onset analysis to middle-class families; its caption says it shows the same pattern as panel A (the full cohort). As read from the figure by the first reader: dependence before 18 against later onset at 1 wave n=9 against 32, at 2 waves n=8 against 10, at 3 or more waves n=17 against 8, with the largest decline (about −0.55 SD) in the adolescent-onset 3-or-more group and changes near zero for adult onset.
key_findings.note: Only the caption could be confirmed by the second reader and the adjudicator; the group sizes and bar heights are single-reader values from the figure (deferred: figure image not viewable). No p values or interaction test are given for panel B.

key_findings.finding: Childhood self-control, described as a precursor of conscientiousness and measured before cannabis use, was unrelated to IQ decline (r = −0.034, P = 0.31); with self-control added, the trend was β = −0.151 (t = −4.38, P = 0.0001).
key_findings.note: For t = −4.38 with about 870 degrees of freedom the two-sided P is about 0.00001 (editors' calculation), so the printed P = 0.0001 should read P < 0.0001.

key_findings.finding: The reply's account of Daly's letter: Daly's own test in the National Child Development Study did not support his conscientiousness hypothesis; his exposure variable did not capture age of onset or persistence, and personality was measured at 50, after cannabis use.

The authors state that observational studies cannot prove causation, list the strategies they used to approach causal inference (temporal order, dose-response, within-individual change, informant reports, exclusion of artefacts, testing rival explanations) and argue that statistical control for confounders needs a theoretical rationale, citing Meehl (1971).
The reply states without showing data that the abilities more susceptible to SES-related effects did not show worse decline.

reporting_issues.issue: The SES measure is not defined (scale, cut-offs, age at measurement); the class sizes, the number of adolescents who used cannabis and the cohort's share of low-SES families are not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 23% figure and the χ2 test cannot be interpreted without the base rate; claims should cite the χ2 and the coefficients, not the 23%.

reporting_issues.issue: β is not defined (standardized or not) and no confidence intervals are reported for any model.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the stability of the coefficient can be cited, not its size in IQ points.

reporting_issues.issue: The self-control-adjusted model is printed as t = −4.38, P = 0.0001, while the other models with t of −4.45 and −4.58 are printed P < 0.0001; with about 870 degrees of freedom t = −4.38 gives P of about 0.00001 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor rounding inconsistency; the conclusion is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter says low-SES children's IQs did not change from the beginning of schooling, but its Fig. 1 starts at age 7 and shows no group sizes or error bars.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure supports stability from 7 to 38, not from school entry; the critical test of Rogeberg's model is the correlation of SES with adolescent-to-adult change (r = −0.006). The text part is confirmed by the second reader and the adjudicator; the figure details (start at age 7, no group sizes or error bars) rest on the first reader's viewing (deferred: figure image not viewable).

reporting_issues.issue: The adjusted models are compared with the 2012 sex-only model (t = −4.45) rather than with the 2012 multivariable model (t = −2.20).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the association survives SES, self-control and other substance dependence together is not reported.
